We implemented a carbon-aware scheduling extension that adjusts EAS energy coefficients based on grid carbon intensity signals. During benchmarking, we see a 35% regression in Geekbench multi-core score compared to stock EAS. The scheduler is over-aggressively packing tasks onto LITTLE cores even when thermal headroom exists on big cores.

ftrace sched_switch + energy model:
  <idle>-0 [000] 200.100: sched_switch: prev_pid=0 next_pid=1842 next_comm=geekbench
  <idle>-0 [000] 200.101: energy_model: pd=LITTLE cap=446 power=120 carbon_coeff=1.0
  <idle>-0 [000] 200.101: energy_model: pd=BIG    cap=1024 power=800 carbon_coeff=3.2
  geekbench-1842 [000] 200.150: sched_migrate_task: pid=1842 dest_cpu=1 (LITTLE)
  geekbench-1843 [001] 200.151: sched_migrate_task: pid=1843 dest_cpu=2 (LITTLE)

carbon_scheduler sysfs:
  /sys/devices/system/cpu/carbon_aware/enabled: 1
  /sys/devices/system/cpu/carbon_aware/grid_intensity: 450 (gCO2/kWh)
  /sys/devices/system/cpu/carbon_aware/big_penalty_factor: 3.2
  /sys/devices/system/cpu/carbon_aware/thermal_override: 0

The carbon penalty factor of 3.2x on big cores makes them appear 3.2x more expensive to EAS. How should we tune this to preserve performance for latency-sensitive workloads?
